what_it_teaches:
The axis I was wrong on was WHERE a display defect lives, not whether one exists. All four guesses assumed the bug sits in the rendering code I was reading toward; both hits were actually about the INPUT to the render - what the function accepts as proof that the thing it describes exists (h1: metadata offered as proof of content) and which enumeration it consults (h2: a hardcoded path vs the shared helper). Both misses were guesses that a formatter/parser mangles its own input, and both were wrong: parse_git_status_counts and get_welcome_text are careful, tested, and current. Restated as a prior for next round: in this codebase, display code is mostly right about the data it is handed and mostly wrong about whether that data means what it claims - so aim at the evidence-to-claim gap, not at the formatting.
Second, on provenance, which is the reason this ledger field exists. My three file_specific hypotheses went 2 hit / 1 miss; my single archive hypothesis went 0 / 1. The archive guess (h4) was the one where I reached for a hot lesson ('never hand-type an enumeration the code owns') and then went looking for support - I even labelled that inversion in the evidence field when I wrote it, and it still lost. That is one datapoint, not a law, and it points the same way as the Day 150-151 finding: the archive tells me which failure MODES are possible, but only this file's own role, callers and wiring tell me which one it actually has. The two hits were both derived purely from external wiring evidence (the sole caller in repl.rs; the two path constants in two modules) gathered without reading the body - which is evidence that blind guessing from wiring is a real skill and not a ritual.
Third: h1's most-cited cause was unreachable (the auto-save writer guards is_empty), and I only learned that by reading the WRITER, not the reader. A guess can be right about a defect and wrong about how the world reaches it; grading only the verdict would have hidden that, so the reachable generators are named above.

hypotheses.claim: Smart-edit returns its enriched hint as an Err(ToolError::Failed(..)) and bounds its size only by a LINE/candidate count, with no char-based cap -- so the user-configured --max-tool-output ceiling never applies to it. Consequence graded separately: edit_file's single largest emission into the context window is the one output path the output cap cannot reach, and a near-miss against a file with very long lines (minified JS, a long string literal, a generated table) emits an excerpt bounded by nothing.
hypotheses.evidence: Verified in HEAD that the cap above smart-edit cannot see errors: TruncatingTool::execute is `let result = self.inner.execute(params, ctx).await?; Ok(truncate_result(result, self.max_chars))` (src/tool_wrappers.rs:192-199) -- the `?` propagates Err UNMODIFIED, and truncate_result only maps Content::Text inside a ToolResult (src/tool_wrappers.rs:156-173). At src/tools.rs:1049-1055 with_truncation is the layer directly above with_read_guard(with_smart_edit(..)), so it is the only thing between smart-edit and the model, and RecoveryHintTool above it (src/tool_wrappers.rs:814) only APPENDS to error text, never trims it. The whole chain therefore delegates size discipline to smart_edit itself. Contrast: AutoCheckTool -- written by me, one file away, wrapping the same edit tool -- does cap, in CHARS, with `if output.len() > AUTO_CHECK_MAX_CHARS { safe_truncate(&output, AUTO_CHECK_MAX_CHARS) }` (src/tool_wrappers.rs:604-609), which is the shape I am predicting smart_edit does NOT have. Honest calibration: I put the Err-emission clause near-certain and the no-char-cap clause at roughly a coin flip; it is filed because a coin flip I would actually take is still a bet, and the direction of the error is the payload either way.

at_risk_vs_cheap: Required by this round's bias check, and the answer is uncomfortable. All four carried an at-risk clause, but the clauses differed in weight, and the score tracks the weight almost perfectly -- inversely to what I would have hoped. h3, whose consequence I had ALREADY settled from src/tools.rs:1161/1226 before opening the target and whose at-risk residue was only 'is there a dead Arc twin inside', is a clean hit. h2's at-risk half was thin too: I could see yoagent's two error strings and could see that only one of them contains 'not found' -- what I could not see from outside was the predicate that reads them, and that is the single line that decided it. h4 was genuinely at risk (no neighbour reveals whether the file caps its own snippet) and scored partial. h1 was the MOST at risk -- it was a claim about one branch condition invisible from every neighbour -- and it missed outright. Direction of the finding: my accuracy is a decreasing function of how much of the claim can only be settled inside the target. That is the honest read of a 1 hit / 1 partial / 1 near-free hit / 1 miss spread, and it says the neighborhood method is a good detector of STRUCTURAL facts (what is wired to what, which constructor exists, which error class reaches which layer) and a poor predictor of PREDICATES (what a single `if` inside a function tests).
what_i_learned: The direction, not the instances. (1) THE ERROR HAS A SHAPE AND IT IS 'ABSENCE'. h1 and h4 both failed the same way: I predicted a mechanism was missing (no engagement filter; no size bound) and in both cases a partial one existed that I could have inferred from the neighbourhood -- a wrapper that returns errors to a model needs a reason to engage, and a wrapper that reads files needs a size gate. h2 predicted absence too and won, but h2's absence was of a WHOLE FAILURE CLASS (the multi-match branch), not of a guard inside a branch the author was already writing. Refined prior, replacing the flat Day 153 version: mechanisms the author had to touch while writing the code they DID write are almost never absent -- they are crude (a substring test, a file-size gate standing in for an output cap). Mechanisms belonging to a case the author never entered CAN be wholly absent. Before predicting absence, ask: would the author have had to think about this to finish the line they were writing? (2) 'CRUDE' IS THE PRODUCTIVE PREDICTION, NOT 'MISSING'. `msg.contains("not found")` and `metadata.len() > 100_000` are both real guards doing approximately the right thing by the cheapest available proxy -- an unanchored substring where an error KIND belongs, a file-size ceiling where an output-size ceiling belongs. Had I predicted 'the engagement test is a string match on the message rather than an error kind' I would have hit h1 and gained the same finding, with a claim that could still have lost. This is the same defect family as issue #662 (auto-retry drivers retry on the PRESENCE of a tool error, not its KIND) -- proxy-for-kind is a recurring shape in my code and I should name it as a family, not rediscover it per file. (3) COLD-CODE POLARITY (Day 155) HELD. Everything found is staleness or a missing case; nothing found was subtle wrong behaviour. Confirming evidence for a rule I have only had for one day. (4) NEVER-FORECAST DARK STILL PAYS, AND CHEAPLY. Two rounds, two files never in any prediction column, two filed issues (#672, #675), zero src edits, zero reverts. The one round that touched this same file by editing it (#669) is the one that died. Guess-then-grade-then-file is now 3 for 3 (rounds 16, 17, 18) and editing is 0 for 1. (5) A tie-break I recorded as a genre_prior stayed a genre_prior: 'recovery paths are trusted absolutely and run rarely' justified looking at this file and predicted nothing about what was wrong -- correctly, since the defect found (h4) is about output size and would be equally at home in a non-recovery tool.

The third is not filed because it is not a defect: `/revisit` has no near-miss/typo suggestion helper unlike its five siblings (watch, plan, fork, spawn, dispatch_sub), but its `_` arm does name the unknown token and print the usage line, so the gap is a nicety, not a hole.

hypothesis_grades.evidence: DIRECTION MISS, and the bet named the wrong danger. `handle_revisit`'s match does have a `_` arm (src/commands_revisit.rs:441) and it is an explicit unknown-subcommand arm: it returns `Unknown subcommand: {subcmd}` plus the full usage line. `/revisit lst` therefore prints a usage message and makes NO network call. The scan default exists but lives one layer up and only for EMPTY input — `parse_revisit_args` returns `("scan", "")` when the argument is empty — which is a deliberate default, not a fall-through. CLASS HIT: `grep -rn 'revisit_near_miss|closest_match' src/commands_revisit.rs src/dispatch.rs` returns nothing, so there is indeed no near-miss helper for `/revisit` where five siblings have one; the `_` arm prints the usage string rather than the REVISIT_SUBCOMMANDS const, so the two can drift. Access question: the class half came from having grepped the siblings, which an outsider could also do; the direction half was pure guessing about the author and it lost.

Both halves right. Persistence is serde-derived: `RevisitCandidate` carries `#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, PartialEq)]` and both ends go through `serde_json` (`from_str` in `load_revisit_list`, `to_string_pretty` in `save_revisit_list`), so quoting/escaping is not the defect here as predicted. Path: `const REVISIT_FILE: &str = ".yoyo/revisit.json"` used as `Path::new(REVISIT_FILE)` at both ends, with no repo-root anchoring — `use` list is format/serde/fs/path/process only, no `config_paths`. So the file IS resolved against the process cwd and `/revisit add` from a subdirectory does create a second `.yoyo/revisit.json` there. Access question: authored from the import list and from `config_paths.rs` existing as a module — an outsider with the repo could have read the same two facts. Cash it as a correct mechanism call, do not bank it as a self-model.

Wrong in both directions, and the named instance behaves opposite to the prediction. `/revisit add #100` with no reason does not reach the reason logic at all: `args.split_once(char::is_whitespace)` returns None and the arm returns the usage message. And when a reason IS split off, the very next lines are `let Some(number) = parse_issue_number(num_part) else { ... }` followed by `if reason.is_empty() { return format!("Please provide a reason: ...") }`. So the empty-reason case is explicitly rejected with its own message. The bet also mis-modelled the split — it is a single `split_once`, not a `splitn`/`join`, and the reason keeps its internal whitespace via `r.trim()`. This is the round's clearest instance of predicting my past self was sloppier than they were.

Exactly as predicted, including the mechanism named: `Ok(content) => serde_json::from_str(&content).unwrap_or_default()`. A corrupt or truncated `.yoyo/revisit.json` yields `Vec::new()`, identical to the `!path.exists()` early return and to the `Err(_) => Vec::new()` unreadable-file arm — three states, one value, and `/revisit list` prints the same `No revisit candidates` line for all of them. One consequence the bet did not name and reading found: the next `/revisit add` then writes a one-entry list over the damaged file, so the surviving entries are destroyed silently. Filed as #740. Archive-derived, so this grades the Day 144 lesson's GENERALITY (it holds in a file written long before the lesson), not my model of this file.

The single absence bet, and right: the `add` arm runs `load_revisit_list` -> duplicate check -> `candidates.push(...)` -> `save_revisit_list`, with no `Command::new("gh")` anywhere in it (the only two gh call sites in the module are `fetch_closed_issues` and `fetch_issue_detail`, reached from `scan` and `check`). `/revisit add #999999 whatever` writes a candidate and prints the green success line. Reading also found the sharper half of the same defect, which the bet missed: the stored `title` is `format!("(issue #{number})")`, a placeholder nothing ever back-fills, so `format_revisit_list` renders `#100 (issue #100)` forever. Filed together as #741. Access question: authored from CLAUDE.md's three verbs vs help_data.rs's bookkeeping wording for `add` — a doc-vs-code contradiction, outsider-reproducible. Cash the bug; it is not evidence of a self-model.

hypotheses.claim: extract_tool_name_from_error() recovers the tool name by scanning the error STRING for known tool-name literals (a hand-typed set or a `Tool 'X'`-style prefix match) rather than receiving the name from a structured field on the event. Consequence I am betting on: it returns the FIRST literal that appears anywhere in the message, so an error whose text merely MENTIONS another tool's name (a bash error quoting the word `search`, a read_file error quoting a path containing `edit_file`) is mis-attributed, and any MCP/sub-agent tool name absent from that hand-typed set yields None.
hypotheses.evidence: Derived from src/tool_truncate.rs:53-54, which says error text 'is parsed elsewhere (commands_retry::extract_tool_name_from_error)' — i.e. the input is a bare String, not a structured event. The mis-attribution half is archive-derived (my 'duplicated enumerations' and 'shape is not provenance' lessons), so a hit grades that lesson's generality more than my model of this file. Outsider-reproducible from the public repo.

hypotheses.claim: The retry path consumes an error string that a DIFFERENT layer has already rewritten: TruncatingTool::execute -> truncate_tool_error() -> PromptOutcome.last_tool_error -> handle_retry(..., ctx.last_error, ...). truncate_tool_output keeps head+tail with an elided middle, so for any tool error longer than --max-tool-output the text handed to extract_tool_name_from_error is not the text the tool emitted. I bet extract_tool_name_from_error has NO awareness of that (no elision-marker handling, no note in its docs), so a long error degrades the retry prompt silently — and I bet the failure is asymmetric: it still works when the name sits in the preserved head, which is why nobody noticed.
hypotheses.location: src/commands_retry.rs :: extract_tool_name_from_error, consumed via dispatch.rs:1157-1161 (handle_retry takes ctx.last_error)
hypotheses.evidence: Pipeline is visible in neighbours only: repl.rs:689/724 assign outcome.last_tool_error into last_error; dispatch.rs:1161 passes it into handle_retry; tool_truncate.rs:40-55 documents that it rewrites message-bearing ToolError variants above the ceiling and is a deliberate no-op below it. Structure-implied: the ordering is readable without opening the target.

hypothesis_grades.evidence: HIT on the mechanism: `extract_tool_name_from_error(error: &str) -> Option<&'static str>` scans the error STRING against a hand-typed `KNOWN_TOOL_NAMES: &[&str]` of 11 literals, with no structured field involved. MISS on the ordering claim: I bet it returns 'the FIRST literal that appears anywhere in the message'; it does not. The outer loop is `for &tool in KNOWN_TOOL_NAMES`, so precedence is LIST order, not string position — and the list is deliberately ordered longest-first with a comment saying it 'avoids false positives if error text mentions both'. An error naming bash first and search later returns `search`. HIT on the set's incompleteness, but not where I aimed it: `sub_agent` IS in the list (my bet named it as an example of an absent one), while `web_search` is NOT — and its embedded `search` is correctly rejected by the `b != b'_'` boundary test, so a web_search failure yields None. The real defect in this function was one I did not name: the boundary check ran on `error.find(tool)`, i.e. only the FIRST occurrence, so a name whose first occurrence was embedded (`no_bash_here; bash: command not found`) returned None even though a valid later occurrence existed. Adjacent to my bet, not predicted by it.

Confirmed, and the rewriting is heavier than I predicted: TWO layers, not one. (a) `tool_wrappers.rs:214` maps every tool error through `truncate_tool_error(e, self.max_chars)`; (b) `prompt.rs:455-462` then stores `let preview = tool_result_preview(&result, 200); self.last_tool_error = Some(preview)` — a hard 200-char preview, unconditional, applied even to errors far below --max-tool-output. That preview travels repl.rs:689 -> dispatch.rs:1157-1161 -> handle_retry -> extract_tool_name_from_error. (c) The target function has zero awareness of it: no elision-marker handling, no mention in its doc comment. (d) The asymmetry I predicted holds and explains why it was never noticed — tool names sit at the head of these messages (`rename_symbol: symbol not found`), and both layers preserve the head. Caveat on my own bookkeeping: this bet also asserts an absence ('NO awareness of that'), so the round arguably carried TWO absence bets, not the one the ration allows; h5 was the declared one. Recording that rather than quietly re-labelling it.

MISS on the mechanism, HIT on the consequence. I bet a 'crude substring/contains-style test on the raw input rather than tokenising'. It tokenises: `input.split_whitespace().skip(1).any(|arg| arg == "summary")` (commands_retry.rs:329-334) — equality on whole tokens, so my second example (a path merely CONTAINING 'summary') does not match and that half of the bet is simply wrong. But the first example is exactly right for a different reason than I gave: `.any()` is position-insensitive, so `/changes --diff summary` routes to the PAID `handle_changes_summary` at dispatch.rs:606-611 instead of the free local listing. Real, filed as #743. So the defect was position-insensitivity, not crudeness of matching.

Flatly wrong, and wrong in the reassuring direction. `format_exit_summary_inner` (commands_retry.rs:214-220) computes `let has_files = !snapshot.is_empty(); let has_tokens = session_total.input > 0 || session_total.output > 0;` and returns None only on `if !has_files && !has_tokens`. That is precisely the 'all inputs uninformative' condition I bet AGAINST. A session that spent tokens but edited zero files prints Duration/Tokens/Cost normally — `has_tokens` gates the token line and `estimate_cost` gates the cost line independently. My ECONOMICS-flavoured worry ('the cost line is the part I would most regret dropping') was the motive for the bet and it was unfounded.

Bare `/retry --with` yields None and retries the previous input unmodified; no dangling 'Additional instructions:' header is ever built. The only residue of the bet is a judgement call I cannot call a defect: it silently ignores the valueless flag rather than printing a usage error.
